chunks: "Clock stretching is when a target holds SCL low to tell the controller 'wait, I'm not ready'.
Both lines are open-drain, so the controller isn't the only one that can pull SCL low. Normally the controller pulls SCL low, then releases it so the pull-up brings it high.
If the target needs more time, for example a microcontroller target running an interrupt handler, or a sensor finishing a conversion, it holds SCL low after the controller has released it.
Since the bus is a wired-AND, SCL stays low as long as the target wants. When the target lets go, SCL rises, and the controller continues.
So the controller has to do two things correctly: after releasing SCL, it must read it back and wait until it's actually high before starting its high-time count and before sampling or changing data.
A controller that just waits a fixed time will clock while the target is still busy and get garbage.
The cost is speed, since each stretch adds to the byte time, so a 400 kilohertz bus with 50 microsecond stretches per byte behaves like about 124 kilohertz.
And a target that never releases hangs the bus, so SMBus defines a timeout of around 25 to 35 milliseconds."
